name: Polyacrylamide gel
lead: Polyacrylamide gel, in its injectable medical form polyacrylamide hydrogel (PAAG), is a water-based synthetic gel made of cross-linked polyacrylamide. It has been used as a permanent soft-tissue filler, including for facial contouring and for HIV-related facial fat loss, and the same type of material is used in other medical settings such as bulking injections for urinary incontinence and, in a Danish trial, intra-articular injection for knee osteoarthritis.[1][5][6][7][8]

For appearance, the appeal is volume that lasts: a gel placed in the cheeks, lips, chin or lines is meant to give a fuller or smoother contour without the repeat sessions that temporary fillers need. The best-known facial product, Aquamid, has been used for cheek (malar) volumising, lip augmentation and the sunken cheeks of HIV-related facial lipoatrophy.[15] Aquamid is about 97.5 percent water and 2.5 percent cross-linked polyacrylamide, was developed and first marketed by the Danish company Contura, and is approved in several countries in Europe, Asia, the Middle East and Latin America but not in the United States.[15]

Polyacrylamide itself is described as low in toxicity, but its precursor, the acrylamide monomer, is a recognised neurotoxin and carcinogen, and safety concerns about PAAG products have centred on possible residual monomer.[2] The FDA lists non-absorbable fillers as approved only for the nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars, and says removal of permanent fillers can be difficult or impossible.[4]

Published facial experience comes mainly from European series of the Aquamid product, which report high satisfaction alongside a documented rate of complications including nodules, displacement and late inflammation.[15] A registered study following 240 women who had polyacrylamide hydrogel removed from the breast and were reconstructed shows that the material has also been injected for breast augmentation and has needed removal in some patients.[9]

paras: Polyacrylamide is a synthetic polymer of acrylamide units. Wikipedia describes it as a material of low toxicity that has been used as a subdermal filler for aesthetic facial surgery, noting concern about acrylamide contamination.[2] Hydrogels in general are cross-linked polymer networks that absorb large amounts of fluid and resemble living tissue, which is why they are used across biomedicine.[10]

Aquamid is made by polymerising acrylamide monomers with a cross-linking agent and is supplied as a colourless, transparent gel in sterile 1 cc syringes.[15] Because the network does not degrade, histology studies described in the Aquamid literature found cell infiltration into the gel and thin fibrous capsules around it months after injection; the review describes the product as a permanent filler that triggers collagen formation.[15] The same family of materials is used in laboratories as the electrophoresis gels familiar from protein science, which is a different, non-injectable use of the polymer.

Most wrinkle and contour fillers are temporary because the body gradually metabolises them, with effects lasting around six months in Wikipedia's account, and duration varying with skin, injector skill, filler type and activity level.[14] Synthetic fillers such as polyacrylamide, as well as poly(methyl methacrylate), are a different category: they rely on a gel or on particles that remain in the tissue rather than a degradable network, which is why they are called permanent or non-absorbable. Wikipedia lists polyacrylamide among the synthetic polymers used in injectable fillers.[14][2]

For people interested in facial appearance, the appeal of a permanent gel is that a single treatment can add volume to the cheeks, lips, chin or lines without repeat sessions. The corresponding trade-off described by the FDA is that permanent filler cannot easily be taken back if the result is unwanted or a complication appears.[4]

Reported facial sites include the cheeks (deep placement over the cheekbone for volume), lips, nasolabial folds, marionette lines, chin and nose.[15] The intent is a lasting change in contour from a single treatment, which is the main difference from hyaluronic acid products that fade over months.[14][15]
A registered phase 3 study injected polyacrylamide hydrogel into the faces of 100 participants with HIV-related facial lipoatrophy, a condition in which cheeks become hollow, beginning in 2005.[7]

The same material has been studied for urinary incontinence, with a randomised trial comparing it with tension-free vaginal tape, and in anal incontinence and vocal-fold laryngoplasty.[5][6][11][12] A 2024 clinical practice statement on urethral bulking agents notes that patients should be counselled about the lack of long-term efficacy data and the possible need for repeat injections or surgery.[16] A 2024 randomised non-inferiority trial in Denmark compared intra-articular polyacrylamide hydrogel with hyaluronic acid in 239 adults with knee osteoarthritis.[8]

Aquamid was developed and marketed by the Danish company Contura International, which was acquired in 2013 by Speciality European Pharma of London.[15] A 2014 review by Yamauchi says the gel had been in use for soft-tissue augmentation for about two decades, and notes that a 24-month US trial was carried out although the product is not marketed there.[15] Histology work on Aquamid dates to studies in 2003 and 2006, and clinical series from 2003 onward are summarised in the review.[15]

Other branded polyacrylamide gels exist, and the registered Chinese study of breast reconstruction after PAAG removal reflects that injectable polyacrylamide was also used for breast augmentation in some regions.[9]

Facial-filler studies of the Aquamid product report high satisfaction: 93 percent of 251 patients rated results good or satisfactory at one year, a two-year follow-up reported maintained results with no serious adverse events, and a 36 to 60 month follow-up reported 96.5 percent good or very good ratings.[15] A manufacturer-reported comparison of 316 patients against a hyaluronic acid filler (Restylane) found similar effectiveness at six months and a greater improvement with Aquamid at 12 months.[15] In HIV facial lipoatrophy, one study found Aquamid and a polylactic acid filler performed similarly through 96 weeks, another found more than 88 percent improved, and a randomised comparison found autologous fat transfer outperformed Aquamid.[15] Nodules appeared in 37 percent of Aquamid-treated and 41 percent of polylactic acid patients in the first comparison.[15]

The FDA's dermal filler guidance lists nodules, granulomas, infection, migration and vascular injury among filler complications and states that some appear weeks to years after injection and that removal of permanent fillers can be difficult or impossible [4]. A systematic review of delayed complications after tear trough filler included polyacrylamide among its search terms, with most reported cases involving hyaluronic acid, poly-L-lactic acid or calcium hydroxylapatite [13].
A registered Chinese follow-up study of breast reconstruction after removal of injected polyacrylamide hydrogel enrolled 240 participants [9].

Wikipedia's overview of fillers describes common effects as bruising, redness, pain and itching, less common ones as infection and allergic reaction that can leave lumps or scarring, and rare serious ones as vision loss from embolisation into the arteries supplying the eye and delayed skin necrosis.[14]

Complication figures in the Aquamid literature vary by series. In a review of reported experience, one study of 542 patients found complications in 7.7 percent, and a larger malar series of 1,306 patients reported unevenness, nodules, pain or gel displacement in about 8.4 percent.[15] A series of 98 patients seen with complications described inflammation in 52 percent, asymmetry in 32 percent, abscess or infection in 11 percent and displacement in 8 percent, with one case of anaphylaxis.[15] A study of 10 patients described delayed immune-mediated reactions beginning about 10 months after injection on average.[15] Culture work in complicated cases found skin bacteria in 98 percent of them and none of the controls, a finding that led to interest in biofilm, and one group reported that prophylactic antibiotics lowered inflammation and infection from 7 to 2 percent.[15]

Removal is described as harder than for hyaluronic acid products, which can be dissolved with an enzyme. In one series, drainage and irrigation removed product in some patients but others could not be fully cleared and some relapsed, and in another series 23 of 24 patients required surgical extraction.[15]

Reviews of filler complications generally note that adverse effects can appear weeks to years after injection and that permanent materials leave the injector without an easy way to reverse them, a contrast the FDA draws with absorbable products.[4][14]

In the United States, fillers are regulated as medical devices and must be prescribed and administered by a licensed provider; the FDA states that non-absorbable fillers are approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars.[4][14] In the UK and European Economic Area, fillers are non-prescription medical devices that need a CE mark, which certifies production standards rather than demonstrated efficacy, and more than 140 products are on the market.[14] China's drug regulator has issued guidance on injectable fillers.[14] Debate continues over who counts as a qualified injector.[14]

Temporary alternatives include hyaluronic acid, which can be dissolved with hyaluronidase, calcium hydroxylapatite and poly-L-lactic acid, and other permanent or semi-permanent options include poly(methyl methacrylate) microspheres and fat transfer.[14][15] In the HIV lipoatrophy comparisons, autologous fat transfer outperformed Aquamid in one randomised study.[15]

Human studies of facial use consist mainly of the Aquamid series described above, which report satisfaction rates from 93 percent at one year to 96.5 percent at 36 to 60 months and complication rates of about 7.7 to 8.4 percent in large series, plus a registered 100-participant HIV lipoatrophy trial.[7][15]

Outside aesthetics, a randomised trial of 239 adults with knee osteoarthritis found a mean WOMAC pain change of -18.5 with polyacrylamide hydrogel versus -14.8 with hyaluronic acid at 26 weeks, within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin.[8] A three-year follow-up of a randomised trial compared polyacrylamide hydrogel injection with vaginal tape for stress urinary incontinence, and a study reported voice outcomes after laryngoplasty.[5][11]

timeline.event: Hyaluronic acid, the usual temporary filler material, is first isolated in 1934 by Meyer and Palmer, background to the later permanent synthetic gels.[17]
Early clinical series and histology of Aquamid (Lemperle 2003) describe its slow dissipation and fine fibrous capsules.[15]

Registered phase 3 study of polyacrylamide hydrogel in HIV-related facial lipoatrophy begins (100 participants); a multicentre Aquamid study of 251 subjects reports 93 percent good or satisfactory outcomes at one year.[7][15]
Retrospective study of 1,306 malar augmentation patients reports complications in 8.4 percent.[15]
Aquamid's developer Contura is acquired by Speciality European Pharma; a case-control study links complicated cases to bacterial biofilm.[15]
Yamauchi review of Aquamid published, noting use for about two decades and no US marketing.[15]
Three-year follow-up of polyacrylamide hydrogel versus vaginal tape in stress incontinence published.[5]
Danish randomised trial of intra-articular polyacrylamide hydrogel versus hyaluronic acid in knee osteoarthritis published.[8]

card.summary: A permanent synthetic gel filler with little published cosmetic evidence in these sources; removal can be difficult.
card.note: Permanent fillers can be hard to remove; concerns centre on residual acrylamide monomer.

quick.overview:
Polyacrylamide gel is a water-rich synthetic gel that has been injected as a permanent filler for facial contouring and fat loss, and is also used in medicine for incontinence and, experimentally, knee osteoarthritis.

The sources contain few studies of its cosmetic use and no forum discussion. Evidence in other uses does not establish how it performs as a face filler.
quick.mechanism: The gel stays in place and adds volume as a non-absorbable bulking material.
quick.risks: Polyacrylamide is described as low in toxicity, but the acrylamide monomer is a neurotoxin and carcinogen, and contamination is a stated concern. The FDA says permanent fillers can cause nodules, migration and late complications and can be difficult or impossible to remove.
